empty-ledger — first-run case where weak_spots.json doesn't exist yet; read_weak_spots() returns [] gracefully so the loop still runs (study-buddy)

handler-vs-decorated-tool — @tool decorator returns an SdkMcpTool object, NOT a callable async function; smoke tests must access .handler to invoke the underlying implementation (recipe-companion smoke_test repair, 2026-06-08)

predicate-vs-signal — model text 'RESEARCH COMPLETE' is a hint, NOT part of the goal predicate; predicate trusts the tool-call log only. mac-advisor turn 1 emitted 'RESEARCH COMPLETE' but conflict_resolved=False, so predicate stayed False — text signal is checked separately as a hint, not as truth (mac-advisor main.py · reinforces Cycle 3 carry-gap)

permission-mode-dontAsk-enforces-palette — allowed_tools alone is a *hint*; permission_mode='dontAsk' is what makes it a *control*. Without dontAsk, the model can still attempt out-of-palette tools and the SDK will prompt; with dontAsk, any out-of-palette call is silently denied (mac-advisor, turn 2 — model tried synthesize_recommendation during research and got blocked)

side-channel-mock-state — when tool implementations need to signal events to the agent loop (e.g. 'a price drop happened'), tool impls write flags to a module-level dict (_mock_state); the agent loop reads the dict after each send_turn() returns and prints the corresponding banner. Cleanest pattern when the SDK boundary hides per-tool returns from the loop (mac-advisor main.py:178)

indian-rupee-formatting — Python's f-string `:,` formatter uses US grouping (₹249,900), not Indian lakh notation (₹2,49,900). For Indian market amounts, format manually: last 3 digits, then comma every 2 digits (mac-advisor _inr() helper)

phase-handoff-instruction-leak — when the agent loop detects a conflict and prints the remediation step to the terminal, the *model* doesn't see that printed line — only the structured state dict injected into the next turn's context does. If the remediation isn't in the dict, the model has no idea what to do next. Carry over remediation as a structured 'pending_clearance' field, not just a binary unresolved flag (mac-advisor Cycle 4 design gap — surfaced in Phase F2 Probe 1)

corrupt-response — when a sub-researcher's query() call returns malformed, empty, or unparseable JSON, treat it as low-confidence (confidence=0.0, gap=True) rather than crashing the loop; the sub-researcher still delivers a report to the main agent so the run can continue (research-lead main.py:523)

hook-input-is-a-dict — the SDK passes PreToolUse and PostToolUse hook input_data as a plain Python dict, not as an object with named attributes. getattr(input_data, 'tool_name', '?') always returns '?' (dicts have no such attribute). Use dict.get('tool_name') instead, or a _get_field() helper that branches on isinstance(obj, dict). This caused all MCP tool calls to hash to ('?', '{}') and be denied as duplicates of the ToolSearch call that fired first. (morning-spark Cycle 6 — discovered on first run; fixed with _get_field helper)

dontAsk-requires-allowed-tools — permission_mode='dontAsk' without an explicit allowed_tools list silently denies all MCP tools at the SDK permission layer — AFTER PreToolUse fires ALLOW. From the output this is invisible: PreToolUse prints ALLOW, a ToolResult UserMessage appears, but the result contains a permission denial, PostToolUse never fires, and the model says 'the tool was denied.' Harness tools (e.g. ToolSearch) are auto-allowed and bypass the check; only MCP tools registered on your server are affected. Fix: add allowed_tools=[list all mcp__server__tool_name strings] to ClaudeAgentOptions when using dontAsk. (morning-spark Cycle 6 — discovered on second run; fixed with ALL_ALLOWED constant)

probes_asked: Probe 1 (two-gate problem) — 'In a production agent, you'll often have multiple independent control layers — hooks, permission modes, rate limits, external API auth. If one of them silently fails, what would you need in the runtime output to catch it fast? What did this run's output tell you, and what did it not tell you?'

Probe 2 (PostToolUse as execution proof) — 'Six spans were written in run 3. If you opened morning-spark_spans.jsonl right now and one of the six entries had result_length: 0 — what would that tell you? What would you check next?'

Probe 3 (the guard that never fired / act-strategy) — 'If you were designing morning-spark for a production environment where the real weather API sometimes returns a 503 error — how would you modify the PreToolUse guard to handle that case? Should the guard allow a retry of the same tool with the same parameters, or should that be handled somewhere else entirely?'
strengths: Observability design (Probe 1 — STRONG) — Ram identified that stage-level logging is the fix: each gate in the pipeline should emit a structured log entry so a silent failure leaves a breadcrumb trail. This is distributed tracing applied to agent pipelines — the right production engineering frame, reached without scaffolding.

Execution vs empty result (Probe 2 — CORRECT) — Ram correctly identified that result_length: 0 means the tool ran but returned nothing useful — execution happened (PostToolUse fired), but the fetch produced no content. Understands the distinction between 'tool ran' and 'tool returned useful data.'

Act-strategy adaptation applied independently (Probe 3 — STRONG) — Ram said 'call a different weather tool' without any prompting. This is the Cycle 5 act-strategy gap applied to a new context without scaffolding: when a resource fails, change the resource (different tool), not the retry count. Gap from Cycle 5 is now demonstrably closed.
gaps: Probe 2 stopped at diagnosis — Ram answered 'what does result_length: 0 mean' correctly but didn't extend to 'what would you check next' (look at result_preview in the span, check the tool impl for the error path, check if the MCP server received the call). Diagnosis without remediation path.

Cost economics (carried from Cycles 2–6, still deferred) — $0.71 for a single clean run; first successful run cost has now been observed, but explicit daily/monthly dollar-math drill again not completed.

runtime_surprises: Goal met in a single turn with 0 denials — the model called all 5 tools in the correct dependency order without any coaching from the PreToolUse guard. The guard existed but never needed to fire. A clean run makes the dedup guard invisible.

Model called fetch_date and fetch_headline in the same response (parallel tool calls). The SDK fired their hooks independently and returned two ToolResults. The parallel calling was the model's own autonomous choice — the system prompt didn't prescribe it.

The two-gate permission bug (dontAsk without allowed_tools) produced uniquely deceptive output in run 2: PreToolUse showed ALLOW, a ToolResult UserMessage appeared, but PostToolUse never fired and the model said 'The weather tool was denied.' The silence between ALLOW and execution was the entire diagnostic — not an error message, just absence of the next expected print line.

Sub-agent interface contract (Probe 3 — STRONG) — Ram named task/boundary/input/output as the defining elements of a sub-agent unprompted: 'Sub-agents typically have a task, a boundary, what input to get and what output to give.' The O-R-A loop detected correctly; the act step needed a strategy change (different source, different query), not a retry. Gap: knowing that observe-a-gap → re-dispatch is insufficient when the re-dispatch doesn't change what it looks at.

run_result.root_cause_of_no_recommendation: phase-handoff instruction leak — the code-side O-R-A loop detected the thermal conflict and computed the remediation step ('call analyze_thermal with sustained_load workload') and printed it to the terminal. But the model's next-turn context received only the binary flag conflict_resolved=False, not the structured remediation instruction. From turn 3 onward the model repeated 'nothing to do' because it had no way to know what to do. Cap fired correctly as a principled stop. NOT an agent failure — a state-propagation design lesson.

probes_asked: Probe 1 (concept-first register, anchor: [CONFLICT DETECTED] remediation line vs [LOOP FEEDBACK] state injection) — Analyst writes resolution note in appendix; meeting runs from executive summary; conflict sits unresolved. How would you redesign the process so the resolution instruction reaches the person who needs to act on it?

Probe 2 (concept-first register, anchor: model attempted synthesize_recommendation in research and got blocked) — Difference between telling an agent 'please don't synthesize until research is complete' versus making synthesis structurally impossible during research. When would you care about that difference?

Probe 3 (concept-first register, anchor: 🏁 EXIT: research cap — 8/8 turns) — From a client management perspective, how would you handle 'goal met' versus 'cap reached' outcomes differently? Does it matter that the agent labelled WHY it stopped?

Probe 4 (concept-first register, anchor: [LOOP FEEDBACK] state re-injection each turn) — Every conversation with the model starts fresh. The agent re-briefs each turn. If you were building an agent that needed to keep working on the same problem across days, not turns, what would you want it to do differently?
strengths: Clearance-register / pre-condition-log pattern (Probe 1) — Ram independently named the FS-consulting pattern that solves this: a gateway between phases that documents what is blocking readiness, so the remediation travels with the work. Direct mapping to the structured-state fix; reached without scaffolding.

Structural enforceability as compliance control (Probe 2) — Ram framed permission_mode='dontAsk' in regulatory terms: 'segregation of duties enforced at the system level, because soft instructions are only as strong as the person following them.' Named auditability + traceability as second-order benefits. Production engineering frame.

Execution-success vs goal-success distinction (Probe 3) — Ram cleanly separated 'the agent executed correctly' from 'the agent achieved its purpose.' Recognized goal-met → delivery process, cap-reached → debrief/recalibration. Most engineers struggle with this; Ram named it crisply.

Episodic memory unprompted (Probe 4) — Ram named 'episodic memory' (literal correct term in the agent literature) before any framing. Named both write-side and read-side selectivity. Connected directly to forthcoming rung-7+/rung-8 capabilities.
gaps: Pre-run inspection of the state-propagation surface — Ram (and the design) didn't anticipate that the code-side remediation print would not reach the model. Reinforces that the LLM only sees what's in its context window; printing to stdout teaches the human, not the agent. Worth surfacing pre-run on the next agent whose loop computes mid-run state changes.

Cost economics (still carried from Cycle 2) — touched conceptually via Probe 4 (memory + cost across days) but the explicit daily/monthly $-math drill was again deferred. Mac-advisor cost $1.87 for one cap-exit run; high-signal evidence for a focused drill.
learning.recall_question_next_cycle: In mac-advisor, the code-side O-R-A loop saw the conflict and computed the right next step — but printed it to the terminal, not into the model's next-turn brief. probes_asked: Probe 1 (tool chain capability) — In Cycle 2 the model sent one action per response and Python dispatched each call. Here it chained 9 tool calls in a single response. What can the agent do in rung 4 that it couldn't in rung 3?

Probe 2 (memory layer persistence) — After a full Python restart, which of the three memory layers survives: conversation history (ClaudeSDKClient), pantry contents (pantry.json), shopping list (shopping_list.json)?

Probe 3 (predicate vs model_done text signal) — The agent has both a goal predicate checking the tool call log AND a model_done signal reading the model's response text. Why both? What breaks if you remove the predicate?
strengths: Tool chain capability (Probe 1) — Ram correctly identified that the agent makes decisions on the fly and chains from ingredient to ingredient without Python controlling each step. Deepened to: model holds the thread; Python doesn't see the tool sequence until the model is done. Correct operational sense of rung 4.

Memory layer structure (Probe 2, self-corrected) — Correctly identified conversation history (SESSION) resets and pantry contents (APP, disk) persists. Initial flip on shopping list (assumed ephemeral) corrected quickly once disk-backed pattern pointed out.
gaps: Predicate-vs-signal reliability (Probe 3 needed scaffolding) — Ram did not independently reach the insight that language is unreliable as a completion signal. Required a concrete failure scenario before the two-mechanism distinction became clear. Insight landed after framing, not before.

main.py not yet run — Environment dependency issue (claude_agent_sdk not installed in PyCharm venv) blocked the actual agent run. Probes answered conceptually. The 9-tool chain, [TOOL CHAIN] label, and four exit paths have not been observed in actual terminal output.

learning.recall_question_next_cycle: In recipe-companion, the predicate trusted the tool call log and the text signal trusted the model's words. Question: if you restricted the model to only two tools mid-session, what would need to change in the goal predicate to stay accurate?
